atlas-qa.0001: A small, fast-registering business centre: the Qatar Financial Centre had over 4,700 firms by June 2026, with technology the largest group of new ones, and the Global Financial Centres Index ranks Doha 52nd. Graduate evidence is thin: the graduate programmes of the sovereign fund and of QatarEnergy are for Qataris, and no source read gives jobs by role. Read the UK’s advice on regional attacks.
atlas-qa.0003: The Qatar Financial Centre reports firm registrations, not jobs or roles, so finance is rated strong on those registrations and the Global Financial Centres Index, not on hiring.
atlas-qa.0004: Qatar’s labour law, Qatarisation rules and sponsorship practice for graduates are fully verified in visas_immigration/qatar/qatar_visas_immigration_guide.md.
atlas-qa.0005: Entry for EU passports and tax were not researched; average pay is whole-country and by activity, with no entry pay and no figure for Doha alone.
atlas-qa.0006: Qatar publishes no city GDP or rent series, and the Doha population is the 2020 census base for the municipality, not the wider built-up area.
atlas-qa.0007: Qatar Airways’ graduate pages could not be read, and no European-graduate employer in Doha was found beyond the free-zone registrations.

atlas-qa.0018: 28,856 paid workers averaging QAR 29,403 a month in 2023
atlas-qa.0020: The Qatar Investment Authority’s one-year Journey graduate programme requires a Qatari national or the child of a Qatari mother; its international hiring is for highly experienced specialists.
atlas-qa.0021: The Qatar Financial Centre onboarded 1,135 firms in the first half of 2026, 37% more than a year earlier, for a total of over 4,700; the largest groups of new firms were technology and innovation (544), media (173) and consulting and professional services (166).
atlas-qa.0022: The UK Foreign Office reports strikes and retaliatory attacks by Iran in the region, Qatar included, since 8 July 2026, and warns of flight cancellations and airspace closures; it does not advise against travel to Qatar as a whole.
atlas-qa.0023: The Global Financial Centres Index 40 (September 2026) ranks Doha 52nd of 117 financial centres (48th in the March 2026 edition), fifth in the Middle East and Africa after Dubai (9th), Abu Dhabi (13th), Casablanca (38th) and Riyadh (46th); Kuwait City is 60th.
atlas-qa.0024: Startup Genome’s 2026 report counts over 300 technology start-ups in Qatar, which raised $58.7 million (QAR 214 million) of venture funding in 2025, nearly double the year before, with 93% of deals at early stage and more than 22 incubators and innovation platforms.
atlas-qa.0025: Qatar’s real GDP grew 2.9% in the third quarter of 2025 against QAR 180.9 billion a year earlier, with non-hydrocarbon activities up 4.4% and 15 of 17 economic activities growing.
atlas-qa.0026: In 2023 Qatar’s 28,856 paid workers in financial and insurance activities averaged QAR 29,403 a month and its 25,965 in information and communication QAR 28,517, against QAR 11,025 for all 2,171,062 paid workers (author’s weighting of the male and female averages).
atlas-qa.0027: The National Planning Council’s open data give Doha municipality 1,186,023 residents, about 40% of the country, from the 2020 census base that its tables repeat for 2020 to 2024.
atlas-qa.0028: Standard employment contracts in Qatar are registered in Arabic and English on the Ministry of Labour portal, EY's Doha graduate programme for nationals asks for excellent written and verbal communication in Arabic and English, and Qatar Living's CV guide says Arabic matters more for government, semi-government and some customer-facing roles; no source measured English at work.
atlas-qa.0029: Graduate recruiting in Qatar runs on university fairs rather than one national season: the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies held its 9th fair on 21 January 2026 with about 30 organisations, the Qatar Foundation Alumni Office its Education City Job Fair on 15 February 2026 for Qatar Foundation students and alumni, Lusail University its third fair on 22-23 October 2025, and Qatar University's fair of 11-14 September 2023 had 73 employers; QatarEnergy says its graduate assessment may take up to 90 days.
atlas-qa.0030: Foreign nationals were 83% of Qatar's private workforce and 94% of its total workforce in 2023, the national strategy aims for 20% Qatari participation in the private and semi-private workforce by 2030, and the World Bank's modelled youth unemployment rate for Qatar was 0.559% in 2025; no graduate-specific unemployment or time-to-first-job figure was found.
atlas-qa.0031: QatarEnergy’s graduate pages describe a programme for "recent Qatari graduates", with a selection process that can take up to 90 days, and its vocational and scholarship programmes are for Qataris and children of Qatari women.
atlas-qa.0032: Qatar’s flagship graduate programmes are for Qataris: QIA’s Journey Program requires Qatari nationality or a Qatari mother, QatarEnergy’s graduate track is for “recent Qatari graduates”, and EY’s Doha graduate programme read is open to Qatari nationals only. Law 12 of 2024 makes private employers give priority to Qataris, and foreign nationals were still 83% of the private workforce in 2023, so foreign graduates are hired into roles outside the nationalisation scheme, mostly by international firms that sponsor the permit.
atlas-qa.0033: Direct application or recruiter, with the employer as sponsor
atlas-qa.0034: No survey ranks the routes in Qatar. Aetna’s relocation guide says people outside Qatar usually apply online or through an agency, and may be interviewed by phone or video by a recruiter in Qatar or by an adviser in their home country; the whole process can take weeks or months and Ramadan or summer slows it.
atlas-qa.0035: The employer then starts the work visa and the Ministry of Labour approval; the worker cannot start on a tourist or visa-waiver status.
atlas-qa.0037: Aetna’s guide calls regional recruitment informal and “all about connections”, and says word of mouth often finds the next job once you are employed. It is a relocation guide, not a survey of graduate hiring.
atlas-qa.0038: Campus recruiting at Qatari universities and the Ouqoul platform
atlas-qa.0039: Qatar University’s annual career fair brought 73 employers from energy, industry, finance, business, education and health to its students on 11–14 September 2023; the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies’ 9th fair on 21 January 2026 had about 30 public and private organisations; Lusail University held its third fair on 22–23 October 2025.
atlas-qa.0040: The Ministry of Labour’s Ouqoul platform is built for private employers to recruit expatriate graduates of Qatari universities for roles outside the nationalisation scheme; its second phase, with graduate registration, is limited to alumni of universities linked to the platform.
atlas-qa.0041: Part-time student jobs and the graduate visa extension (Jusour Sahem)
atlas-qa.0042: Jusour’s Sahem programme offers part-time jobs to students at accredited Qatari universities, and The Peninsula reported in July 2023 that it also offers recent graduates of Qatar-based institutions, aged 18 to 28 and on institution-sponsored residence, a one-year visa extension to look for work.
atlas-qa.0043: The library’s visa guide finds no stand-alone internship visa: a student or graduate from abroad cannot intern on a tourist or waiver status, so the internship route works for those already resident as students.
atlas-qa.0045: QatarEnergy’s graduate track is for recent Qatari graduates and its assessment may take up to 90 days; QIA’s one-year Journey programme requires Qatari nationality or a Qatari mother; EY’s Doha Qatar Graduate Program posting is “for nationals” and runs online assessments, a recorded video interview and a recruitment day before an offer. A foreign graduate cannot use them.
atlas-qa.0046: Aetna’s guide writes its benefits section mainly for intra-company transfers and secondments, with health cover and accommodation; for a graduate this is a later route, after a first job at the group elsewhere. This is our reading.
atlas-qa.0047: There is no national season: graduate fairs fall in January and February (Doha Institute on 21 January 2026, the Education City Job Fair on 15 February 2026) and in autumn (Lusail University on 22–23 October 2025, Qatar University in September 2023).
atlas-qa.0048: QatarEnergy says its graduate assessment may take up to 90 days, so a Qatari applicant starts months before the intended start; the pages read give no opening or closing months for any programme.
atlas-qa.0049: For students at Qatari universities, Jusour’s graduate visa extension gives one year to find a job after graduating.
atlas-qa.0050: Qatar University’s Career Development Center runs the annual fair and a student-employment programme; the Education City Job Fair is organised by the Qatar Foundation Alumni Office for Qatar Foundation students and alumni only, so access to the fairs follows the university you attend.
atlas-qa.0051: Foreign universities do not recruit here: the Ouqoul platform’s graduate side is open only to alumni of Qatari universities. We found no ranking of schools by Qatari employers.
atlas-qa.0052: Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, 9th Career Fair: 21 January 2026, 9:00 to 16:00, about 30 public and private organisations, mainly for its own students and graduates.
atlas-qa.0053: Education City Job Fair 2026: 15 February 2026, organised by the Qatar Foundation Alumni Office for Qatar Foundation students and alumni only.
